## NFL Big Data Bowl: Background

* Premier sports analytics competition, focusing on player tracking data

* Data are collected at 10 Hz using RFID chips placed in player shoulder pads and ball

* Every year the NFL releases a sample a tracking data with a competition theme

* Multiple tracks 

  * college/university/undergraduate 
  
  * open/metric
  
  * coaching, broadcast
  
* Prizes: $100,000 total prize since 2021 (prize distribution may be different for each year)

## NFL Big Data Bowl: Themes

Started in 2019, hosted on Kaggle since 2nd year

* [2019](https://github.com/nfl-football-ops/Big-Data-Bowl): route combinations + rule changes + speed
    
* [2020](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2020): yards gained after receiving a handoff (prediction competition)
    
* [2021](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2021): secondary
    
* [2022](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2022): special teams
    
* [2023](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2023): linemen on pass plays
    
* [2024](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2024): tackling
    
* [2025](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2025): pre-snap
    
* 2026 [prediction](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2026-prediction) & [analytics](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2026-analytics): player movement while the ball is in the air

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

fake_points <- tibble(
  y = 0, 
  x = c(-0.2, 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.9),
  col = c("black", "black", "darkorange", "black", "black", "black"),

)

p_base <- ggplot() +
  theme_void() +
  annotate("segment", x = -0.2, y = 0, xend = 1, yend = 0,

```

# Working with tracking data

## Data prep: Field standardization

* In the raw data, there are 2 play directions (with respect to the offense): left and right

* We need to standardize player tracking coordinates

  * Ensure the offense is always moving in the same direction

  * Helpful for feature engineering and modeling
  
## Data prep: Field standardization

<center>
![](field.png){width=80%}
</center>

## Data prep: Field standardization

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

* First, read in the data<br>(Data files are in the same directory<br>as the slides source file)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_light())
games <- read_csv("games.csv")
plays <- read_csv("plays.csv")
players <- read_csv("players.csv")
player_play <- read_csv("player_play.csv")
tracking <- list.files(pattern = "tracking_week_") |> 
  map(read_csv) |> 
  list_rbind()
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

* Make all plays go from left to right, then flip player direction and orientation 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
tracking <- tracking |>
  mutate(
    # make all plays go from left to right
    x = ifelse(playDirection == "left", 120 - x, x),
    y = ifelse(playDirection == "left", 160 / 3 - y, y),
    # flip player direction and orientation
    dir = ifelse(playDirection == "left", dir + 180, dir),
    dir = ifelse(dir > 360, dir - 360, dir),
    o = ifelse(playDirection == "left", o + 180, o),
    o = ifelse(o > 360, o - 360, o)
  )
```

:::
:::

# Motion type clustering

## Problem formulation

* Problem: provide (unsupervised) labels for the types of motion by receiver

. . .

* What is motion in American football?

. . .

> In gridiron football, motion refers to the movement of an offensive player at the time of the snap. (Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_(gridiron_football)))

. . .

* There are many types of motion (see [here](https://web.archive.org/web/20241224211405/https://www.viqtorysports.com/pre-snap-movement-in-the-offense/))

## Motion example: jet/fly sweep

<center>
![](jet.gif){width=80%}
</center>

## Motion example: orbit

<center>
![](orbit.gif){width=80%}
</center>

## Motion example: exit

<center>
![](exit.gif){width=80%}
</center>

## Clustering strategy

* Strategy: extract features from tracking data, then perform model-based clustering

  * This can be applied to various unsupervised labeling problems in sports (with tracking data)
  
. . .

* Input: features summarizing the trajectory of motion players at
different events during a play, relative to where the center lines up before the snap

. . .

* Feed these features into any clustering algorithm ($k$-means, Gaussian mixture model,...)

. . .

* Inspect results and provide annotations for the motion types

. . .

* Alternative strategy: functional/curve clustering (more advanced; working with full trajectory)

## Clustering features

<center>
![](features.png){width=70%}
</center>

## Clustering features

$\textsf{B}_{\textsf{sideline}}$ : displacement (wrt sideline) between center and motion player at ball snap 

$\textsf{B}_{\textsf{endzone}}$ : displacement (wrt endzone) between center and motion player at ball snap

$\textsf{M}_{\textsf{sideline}}$ : displacement (wrt sideline) between center and motion player at the start of motion 

$\textsf{L}_{\textsf{sideline}}$ : displacement (wrt sideline) between the center and motion player at the moment of<br>crossing the line of scrimmage (LOS)

. . .

* For plays where the motion player NEVER crosses LOS, find the earlier frame of<br>{QB event, 3 seconds after snap}, and use location at that frame in place of $\textsf{L}_{\textsf{sideline}}$
  
* Why 3 seconds? For plays where motion players do cross LOS...
  
  * Plot the distribution of time elapsed between the moments of ball snap and crossing LOS 
    
  * Find a threshold that capture a majority of the values of that distribution

# Clustering

## Clustering (cluster analysis)

* Clustering is a fundamental problem in unsupervised learning

* **Goal**: partition of the observations into different clusters so that observations **within** a cluster are **more similar** to each other

. . .

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"}

**Hard clustering**

* Example: $k$-means, hierarchical clustering
  
* Output hard assignments
  
* Strictly assign each observation to only one cluster
  
:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"}

**Soft/fuzzy clustering** 

* Example: model-based clustering, mixture model

* Output soft assignments
  
* Assign an observation a probability of belonging to each cluster
  
* Provide uncertainty in the clustering results
  
* Incorporate statistical modeling into clustering
  
:::

:::

## Classification vs clustering

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"}

**Classification**

*   Supervised learning

*   We are given labeled (categorical) data

*   Focus on generalizability<br>(i.e. build a classifier that performs well on predicting unseen/test data)

:::

::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"}

**Clustering**

*   Unsupervised learning (often more subjective)

*   We are only given the data points (with no labels)

*   Focus on finding interesting subgroups/structure in the data

:::
:::


## Model-based (parametric) clustering

* Key idea: data are considered as coming from a mixture of underlying probability distributions

. . .

* Assume data are sample from a population with underlying density; estimate density, use its characteristics to determine clustering structure

. . .

* Most popular method: Gaussian mixture model (GMM)

  *   Each observation is assumed to be distributed as one of $K$ multivariate normal distributions

  *   $K$ is the number of clusters/components
  
. . .  
  
* Other variations: skewed normal, Student's-$t$, beta, etc. (as long as it can be estimated)

## Mixture models in general

* Each population subgroup (component/cluster) is represented by some density $f_k(x; \theta_k)$

. . .

* The population density $f(x)$ is a weighted combination (i.e. mixture) of the subgroup densities $$\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \tau_k f_k(x; \theta_k)$$

  * $\tau_k$: **mixture weights**, with $\tau_k \ge 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^K \tau_k = 1$

  * $f_k$: **mixture components**

  * $K$: total number of mixture components (clusters)
  
. . .

* We need to choose the number of components (clusters) $K$ and the weights $\tau_k$, and estimate the parameters $\theta_k$ of the mixture component densities $f_k$


## Gaussian mixture models

* Assume a **parametric mixture model** (with **parameters** $\theta_k$ for the $k$-th component) $$f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \tau_k f_k(x; \theta_k)$$

* The mixture component densities are assumed to be Gaussian with parameters $\theta_k = \{\mu_k, \Sigma_k\}$

. . .

* The covariance matrices $\Sigma_k$ characterize the clusters

  * **volume**: size of the clusters (number of observations)

  * **shape**: direction of variance (which variables display more variance)

  * **orientation**: aligned with axes (low covariance) versus tilted (relationships between variables)
  
. . .  
  
* Each of these (volume/shape/orientation) can be chosen to be the same or different among clusters  

## Covariance constraints

3 letters in model name denote (in order) the volume, shape, and orientation across clusters

<center>
![](covariances.png){height=620}
</center>


## Covariance constraints

<style>
.table-small table {
  font-size: 0.72em;
}
</style>

<center>

::: table-small
| Model | Distribution | Volume    | Shape    | Orientation     |
|-------|--------------|-----------|----------|-----------------|
| EII   | Spherical	   | Equal	   | Equal	  | --              |
| VII   | Spherical	   | Variable  | Equal	  | --              |
| EEI   | Diagonal	   | Equal	   | Equal	  | Coordinate axes |
| VEI   | Diagonal	   | Variable  | Equal	  | Coordinate axes |
| EVI   | Diagonal	   | Equal	   | Variable | Coordinate axes |
| VVI   | Diagonal	   | Variable  | Variable | Coordinate axes |
| EEE   | Ellipsoidal  | Equal	   | Equal	  | Equal           |
| EVE   | Ellipsoidal  | Equal	   | Variable | Equal           |
| VEE   | Ellipsoidal  | Variable  | Equal	  | Equal           |
| VVE   | Ellipsoidal  | Variable  | Variable | Equal           |
| EEV   | Ellipsoidal  | Equal	   | Equal	  | Variable        |
| VEV   | Ellipsoidal  | Variable  | Equal	  | Variable        |
| EVV   | Ellipsoidal  | Equal	   | Variable | Variable        |
| VVV   | Ellipsoidal  | Variable  | Variable | Variable        |
:::

</center>

## Model fitting and selection

* Model fitting is done using an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm

* Since this is a statistical model, we can choose the number of components/clusters $K$ and covariance constraint using the Bayesian Information Criterion ($\textsf{BIC}$) $$\textsf{BIC} = 2\log L(x \mid \theta) - m\log n \,,$$

  * $L(x \mid \theta)$: likelihood of the considered model

  * $m$: number of parameters (e.g. VVV has the most parameters)
  
  * $n$: number of observations

* The BICs are calculated for all candidate models (different combinations of $K$ and covariance constraints), and we select one final model that gives the optimum BIC value

:::aside
<br>
The above $\textsf{BIC}$ is really the $- \textsf{BIC}$ of what you typically see, this sign flip is just for ease
:::


## Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm

* Goal: Given a GMM, we want to maximize the likelihood function with respect to the parameters (means & covariances of the components and mixture weights)

. . .

* First, initialize the model parameters ($\mu_k, \Sigma_k, \tau_k$) randomly

. . .

* Then, alternate between the following two steps (keep repeating until convergence)

    *   **E-step**: estimate $\gamma_{ik}$, the **soft assignments** of observation $i$ belonging to component/cluster $k$
    
    *   **M-step**: re-estimate the model parameters
    
. . .    
    
* Output: $\hat{\gamma}_{ik}$ are the final estimated soft assignments of observation $i$ belonging to cluster $k$

    * We can assign observation $i$ to a cluster with the largest $\hat{\gamma}_{ik}$
  
    * We also get the cluster assignment **uncertainty** of $\displaystyle 1 - \max_k \hat{\gamma}_{ik}$    

## Data preparation

* For illustration purpose, let's only consider plays with one motion player since line set *and* a receiver running route

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
player_play_motion <- player_play |> 
  filter(motionSinceLineset == TRUE & wasRunningRoute == 1) |> 
  add_count(gameId, playId, name = "n_motion") |> 
  filter(n_motion == 1) |> 
  distinct(gameId, playId, nflId)
```

* Get the tracking data for only the players in the above subset of plays

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
tracking_players_motion <- tracking |> 
  inner_join(player_play_motion)
```

## Feature engineering

Coordinate system
  
* `x`: direction of the target endzone
  
* `y`: direction of the sideline

. . . 

Some challenges and decisions

* We don't have the role indicator for who the ball snapper is in the data

  * We could rely on the `position` column in the `players` data and<br>get those whose position is `C` (center)
  
  * This doesn't guarantee that we can identify the snapper for every play<br>(sometimes the guard, tackle, or even long snapper has to snap the ball if the center is injured)

## Feature engineering

* Instead, use these as reasonable proxy for `x` and `y` of the center before the snap

  * Use the `x` for the line of scrimmage

  * Use the `y` for the QB before the snap

    * Use the location at any of `line_set`/`man_in_motion`/`ball_snap`<br>(let's go with `line_set`)

  * Avoid using football location since it can be inaccurate


## Get relevant frames for each play

* Frames of `line_set`, `man_in_motion`, `ball_snap`, and<br>QB event (`pass_forward`, `qb_sack`, `qb_strip_sack`, `fumble`)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
tracking_players_motion <- tracking_players_motion |> 
  group_by(gameId, playId) |> 
  mutate(frame_line_set = frameId[which(event == "line_set")][1],
         frame_man_in_motion = frameId[which(event == "man_in_motion")][1],
         frame_ball_snap = frameId[which(frameType == "SNAP")][1],
         frame_qb_event = frameId[which(event %in% c("pass_forward", "qb_sack", "qb_strip_sack", "fumble"))][1]) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  filter(!is.na(frame_line_set), !is.na(frame_man_in_motion), !is.na(frame_ball_snap), !is.na(frame_qb_event))
```

* Frame when the motion player crosses the line of scrimmage

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
# load nflreadr pbp to get line of scrimmage info (yardline_100) + info about the QB/passer (passer_player_id)
play_context <- nflreadr::load_pbp(2022) |> 
  mutate(old_game_id = as.numeric(old_game_id))

plays_cross_los <- tracking_players_motion |>
  left_join(play_context, by = join_by(gameId == old_game_id, playId == play_id)) |> 
  mutate(x_los = 110 - yardline_100) |>
  filter(frameId >= frame_ball_snap & frameId <= frame_qb_event) |>
  group_by(gameId, playId, nflId) |>
  summarize(frame_cross_los = frameId[which(x > x_los)][1]) |> 
  ungroup()
```

* For plays where the motion player NEVER crosses the line of scrimmage,<br>find the earlier frame of {QB event, 3 seconds after snap}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
plays_never_cross_los <- tracking_players_motion |> 
  distinct(gameId, playId, nflId, 
           frame_qb_event, frame_3s_after_snap = frame_ball_snap + 30) |> 
  mutate(frame_end = pmin(frame_qb_event, frame_3s_after_snap)) |> 
  inner_join(filter(plays_cross_los, is.na(frame_cross_los))) |> 
  select(gameId:nflId, frame_end)

plays_frame_end <- plays_cross_los |> 
  filter(!is.na(frame_cross_los)) |> 
  rename(frame_end = frame_cross_los) |> 
  bind_rows(plays_never_cross_los)

# Why 3 seconds after the snap?
# Plot distribution of time elapsed between snap and crossing LOS for plays with motion players crossing LOS.
# Find a threshold that capture a majority of the values of that distribution.
# 3 sec i.e. 30 frames capture a high proportion of the values. (2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, etc. should all be fine, just needs to be something reasonable)

# plays_cross_los |>
#   inner_join(distinct(tracking_players_motion,
#                       gameId, playId, nflId, frame_ball_snap)) |>
#   mutate(frame_snap_to_cross_los = frame_cross_los - frame_ball_snap) |>
#   ggplot(aes(frame_snap_to_cross_los)) +
#   geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
#   geom_vline(xintercept = 30, linetype = "dashed")
```

## Get relevant frames for each play

* Create a table storing the relevant frames for each play

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
plays_frames <- tracking_players_motion |> 
  distinct(gameId, playId, nflId,
           frame_line_set, frame_man_in_motion, frame_ball_snap) |> 
  left_join(plays_frame_end)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
read_rds("../data/plays_frames.rds") |> 
  head(30) |> 
  rmarkdown::paged_table()
```

## Compute clustering features

* Desiredata: a table with 

  * `gameId`, `playId`, `nflId`
  * 4 clustering features about change in `y`/`x` mentioned earlier

* First, get the location of the QB (passer), in order to approximate `y` for the center before the snap

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
plays_passer <- play_context |> 
  select(gameId = old_game_id, playId = play_id, passer_player_id) |> 
  left_join(select(nflreadr::load_players(), passer_player_id = gsis_id, nflId = nfl_id)) |> 
  select(-passer_player_id) |> 
  inner_join(distinct(plays_frames, gameId, playId))

tracking_passer <- tracking |> 
  inner_join(mutate(plays_passer, nflId = as.numeric(nflId))) |> 
  left_join(play_context, by = join_by(gameId == old_game_id, playId == play_id)) |> 
  mutate(x_los = 110 - yardline_100) |> 
  select(gameId, playId, frameId, x_los, y_passer = y)
```

* Now join, pivot, and calculate all features

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
plays_frames_locations <- plays_frames |> 
  pivot_longer(starts_with("frame_"), 
               values_to = "frameId", 
               names_to = "frame_event",
               names_prefix = "frame_") |> 
  inner_join(tracking_players_motion) |> 
  select(gameId, playId, nflId, frameId, frame_event, x, y) |> 
  left_join(tracking_passer) |> 
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(gameId, playId, nflId),
              names_from = frame_event,
              values_from = c(frameId, x, y, x_los, y_passer),
              values_fn = list) |> 
  unnest(cols = contains("_")) 

plays_clustering_features <- plays_frames_locations |> 
  mutate(x_center_before_snap = x_los_line_set,
         y_center_before_snap = y_passer_line_set, 
         y_change_start = abs(y_man_in_motion - y_center_before_snap),
         y_change_end = abs(y_end - y_center_before_snap),
         x_change_snap = abs(x_ball_snap - x_center_before_snap),
         y_change_snap = abs(y_ball_snap - y_center_before_snap))
```

## Model-based clustering with `mclust`

```{r}
#| echo: false
plays_clustering_features <- read_rds("../data/plays_clustering_features.rds")
tracking_players_motion <- read_rds("../data/tracking_players_motion.rds")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(mclust)
set.seed(1)
motion_gmm <- plays_clustering_features |> 
  select(contains("_change_")) |> 
  Mclust(G = 3:15)
```

```{r}
motion_gmm |>
  summary()
```

## View clustering assignments with uncertainty

* Can also make other pair plots (or do PCA and plot first 2 PCs)

```{r}
# motion_gmm |>
#   plot(what = "classification")

motion_gmm |> 
  broom::augment(plays_clustering_features) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = x_change_snap, y = y_change_snap, color = .class, size = .uncertainty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  theme_light()
```

## What are the clusters?

* We have these clustering results. Can we label them?

. . .

* Idea: plot the trajectory between `man_in_motion` (red) and `ball_snap` (blue) of motion players in each cluster

. . .

* This is just a starting point and can certainly be improved

  * Standardize relative to line of scrimmage, middle of the field/formation, QB location
  
  * Analysis of motion player's position (WR/TE/RB) in each cluster

  * Human validation (e.g. talk to a coach, compare with a real football team's playbook)
  
. . .

* Preview of results: We can see some structural differences between the clusters and probably label some of them (1: orbit?, 2: fly/jet?, 4: glide?, 5: over?, 7: exit? etc.)

## What are the clusters?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
motion_clusters <- motion_gmm |>
  broom::augment(plays_clustering_features) |>
  mutate(curve_id = row_number()) |>
  select(gameId:frameId_end, cluster = .class, curve_id) |>
  left_join(tracking_players_motion) |>
  filter(frameId >= frameId_man_in_motion & frameId <= frame_ball_snap) |>
  mutate(frame_color = ifelse(frameId == frameId_man_in_motion, "red", NA),
         frame_color = ifelse(frameId == frame_ball_snap, "blue", frame_color))

motion_clusters |> 
  ggplot(aes(y, x, group = curve_id)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = I(frame_color)), size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_path(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster, nrow = 2) +
  labs(x = "Along the sideline", y = "Toward the endzone") +
  theme_light()
```


## Trajectory clustering in team sports

* [Miller and Bornn (2017)](https://www.sloansportsconference.com/research-papers/possession-sketches-mapping-nba-strategies), Sloan: possession actions 🏀

* [Gregory (2019)](https://static.capabiliaserver.com/frontend/clients/barca/wp_prod/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/40ba07f4-ready-player-run-barcelona.pdf), Barça: off-ball runs ⚽

* [Chu et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.02423), JQAS: route types 🏈

* [Dutta et al. (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.11373), JQAS: pass coverage types (man/zone) 🏈

* [Eager et al. (2024)](https://www.sloansportsconference.com/research-papers/using-tracking-data-to-build-offensive-line-development-tools), Sloan: pass blocking paths 🏈

* [Nguyen and Yurko (2025+)](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf185), JRSSA: pre-snap motion types 🏈
